The researchers' study of the long-term effects of human smoking on both mental and physical health was published recently in the journal Plos Medicine.
The researchers examined how the use of tobacco products, especially cigarettes, has a significant impact on the overall mental health of smokers and their partners. The study also found that smoking significantly affected mental health in those who quit using cigarettes for 12 months or longer than non-smokers.
"Smoking is a major contributor to poor mental health among smokers," says Dr. Robert R. Skovin, director of the Center for Behavioral Health at Tufts University's Center for Disease Control and Prevention, and senior author of the study. "This study provides evidence that the long-term effects of smoking are not only limited by its negative effects on mental health but also by the risk of depression."
Nicotine does not affect the body's ability to process other chemicals that give rise to mood disorders such as anxiety and depression, but it can cause an array of mental disorders, including schizophrenia, to worsen over time. But the long-term effects of nicotine exposure on mental health have not been studied, so this new study shows that long-term smoking may have more effects on mental health than previously thought.
